utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you. It appears we have a problem with the LiveNote very early on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic. We are now back on track. May we continue the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just going to say that, just before the witness comes in, over the adjournment, someone on the -- working for the OTP had the bright idea of going to the military lexicon, which I wasn't actually aware that we possessed, but we do, but for definitions of "combat" and also "armed conflict." We've uploaded the relevant parts in B/C/S and, just now, the translation into English, and if there was no objection, I may -- I was proposing to ask the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. We trust that you remain able to continue with us. Again, as I said yesterday, if there are any problems, you would -- please don't hesitate to alert us. And before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you of your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, yesterday afternoon, no, yesterday morning, when we concluded, I was asking you about the definition of "combat" and whether it was defined anywhere in military terms. And over the adjournment we've had a look at the military lexicon. Are you familiar with the military lexicon?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of my attachments in the report that I prepared for this Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It may well be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we have up, please -- let's have up the definition of "combat," 20259, and it's tab 110. And I don't think that's it. That looks suspiciously like a log-book to me. It is a log-book. Can we try again? 65 ter 20259. No, I don't think it's a photograph of Sanski Most Police Station either. I think this court is jinxed this afternoon. And hot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we concentrate on -- in B/C/S on "borba." Thank you. And let's highlight the first paragraph, because I'm not too worried about the sea, as Bosnia was a land-locked country, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. "Combat, the basic and most widespread form of combat activity," which, I suppose, doesn't really help much, but still, "carried out directly by individuals, groups and tactical units ... individually or within a battle ... It may be attacking or defending." Modern combat, as opposed to Morden combat, "is characterised by ... large complexity, dynamism and sudden changes of situations ... waged on land ... sea and ... air, along the front," or "...temporarily occupied territory ... in the [sic] rear ... involves all form of arm conflict," - and we'll look at what's -- armed conflict is defined in a minute, and "it is the dominant form of combat activities in the guerrilla's [sic] type of armed conflict and in ... occupied --" temporarily occupied territories. "The elements of combat are movement ... fire ... strike ... For each combat are determined target of activity, forces ... equipment, and the zone of activity ..." And "It can be carried out in any conditions ..." From your experience, General, would that appear to be a definition that you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we -- Your Honours, I suppose we probably ought to ask for it to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why can't this be migrated into the law library?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. Certainly, Your Honour. Oh, well, in fact, it may well be part? It's probably -- I imagine the military lexicon is part of the law -- oh, no, I see head-shaking going on. It's not. Your Honour, I have no strong feelings about this, but I have omitted certain parts. And if anybody wants to ask about, then it probably ought to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we considered that when we were -- when we were complying the -- getting together the law library, but the military lexicon is a very lengthy document, and therefore what I suggest is we don't -- we don't object that certain portions, as Ms. Korner sees fit, certain pages of that lexicon be -- be exhibited, as -- as part of the -- a part of the law library. And we can discuss that over -- that matter over the break, and inform the Trial Chamber accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, as I say, I have no strong feelings? It is, as the General's pointed out, cited on about -- on seven occasions in his report. All right. Can we look, please, next at armed -- the definition of "armed conflict," which is 20260, at tab 111.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Oruzana borba," I think, is "armed conflict."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And armed conflict is defined as the "main substance and form of manifesting war. In a wider sense, using weapons in a conflict between men, groups, organisations, movements, states" -- oh, sorry. I'll read that more slowly. "In a wider sense, using weapons in a conflict between men, groups, organisations, movements, states and other, when one side tries to submit the other to their will by means of physical destruction or coercion - implementation of armed violence. One of the basic functions of armed conflict is destroying the opponent's manpower and equipment." And I, for the moment, I don't think I need to read anything else. Again, General, can I ask if you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Ms. Korner. I would also point out that the same thing applies as to the previous document. Namely, the federal state, at the time, decided that the only danger it was facing was from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In actual fact, all the laws and regulations, General, that related to the military, the use of the JNA, really presupposed that the JNA would be fighting an outside enemy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, those were laws adopted by the highest ranking state bodies in keeping with their powers and authority. I do agree with you that, above all, the document envisaged that any threat to the state would come from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the problems with what happened from 1991 onwards was that nobody -- well, I say nobody. It had not been thought, and these laws and military regulations were being drafted, that there would be an internal armed conflict. And by "internal," I mean within the borders of what was the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Ms. Korner. However, all those laws or single principles applied particularly to situations involving command and principles of command, singleness of command, subordination, resubordination, concerted action, co-operation, all of this applies under any conditions regardless of the type of aggression that occurs, aggression from outside or, indeed, aggression from within.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I'll come back to that because I want to talk about resubordination later. I just want to ask you this before we move on, please: It's clear, isn't it, that combat, combat activity, whether armed combat or -- or ordinary combat, because, as I understand, there's a difference in your language, did not cover an activity such as guarding prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we mentioned combat as a concept previously. I know what problem people who never dealt with military subjects can face in relation to that concept. Combat is the first form of combat operations. Above that is battle. Above battle is operation, as the highest and most complex form of combat activity. What is applied as part of combat are combat procedures and actions. Guarding POWs, is it a procedure or a combat activity? This is an issue regulated by a certain combat document, and this is a subject that I address in my report. I am talking about orders, combat orders, commands and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, combat, it's clear, isn't it, is an actual fight? Once the fight is over, and, as we saw, I think it was 1.000-odd prisoners were taken, combat is completed, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when combat is completed, or, to be more precise, during combat, commanders from company level up have the authority to set up reception centres, and that is where prisoners of war are taken, as well as any war booty. All this is part and parcel of combat, as such. All of this is part and parcel of the war happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Once the prisoners who allegedly had been taken prisoner because they have been in the opposing side are taken to a camp and incarcerated, the combat, which led to their incarceration, is complete, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, all of this is something that is prescribed and determined by a certain enactment, or document, which defines when combat, a battle or particular operation, commences. It also determines what the precise tasks are within that framework, and it also determines when there is an end to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In theory, I'm sure that's wonderful. But as we've seen in some of the documents you've looked at, what happens is that, for example, General Talic or one of his brigade commanders gives an order to take a village. The village is taken. The report is made to the Main Staff, as we saw with the attack on Kozarac. Once that report has gone to the Main Staff, would you accept that the combat has ended?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we -- I'm sorry, can we have the reference and basis for this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- well, I'm sorry, we've dealt with this - I'm not going over it - yesterday. You look at yesterday's transcript. I showed the General the document where we saw that the attack on Kozarac had taken place and the prisoners had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, certain activities are completed. The reporting process continues during combat and after combat is completed. Now that is where I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But as far as the 1.610 persons taken prisoner are concerned, the combat, for them and the persons who were taking them prisoner, has ended, has it not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, therefore, when we they are in a prison camp, like, for example, Manjaca, the guarding of those men is not a combat activity, is it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, per establishment, the organising and the functioning of a POW camp is under the authority of military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that. My simple question is: There is not -- that camp, being guarded with its prisoners, is not a combat activity, is it, within the definition we've looked at of combat or armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go back, I'm afraid, to ask you about one document, the one that you didn't want to read last night, that relates to your question of -- sorry, your assertion about the lack of communication going on within the VRS during the relevant period. So we need, I'm afraid, just to have a brief look, please, at document ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the duty -- the notebook from the duty team, which is 20225, at tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, although it doesn't say it, but it's the 1st K -- it's the 1 K -- or the 5th Krajina Corps, which then became the 1st Krajina Corps, notebook. It is in fact. It is accepted that is what it is. And it's headed: "Duty Team, daily notes on the situation of the battlefield and in the zone of responsibility." Would this have been -- you described that you'd carried out some staff duties. Would this have been the sort of notebook that would have been compiled by staff officers who were on duty and receiving information? Are you familiar with a document like this?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I remember, I said that I was first involved and, at the end of my career, also the leader of duty teams. The primary task of those was to monitor activities across the units and to make sure there was a continuity of command and control whenever the relevant commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you are -- is this the sort of notebook that would be kept; and are you familiar with this type of notebook?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I am looking at the name of the document, and it's difficult for me to judge whether this is a wartime log-book belonging to a command, which currently I cannot identify by looking at this. The other thing it might be was a simple daily report that would help them to compile the overall daily or evening report. So this might be a simple aid that they used to compile the overall daily combat report at the end of the day. This report would then be submitted to their superior command, covering activities and everything that went on in any of the units under that particular command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have a look at a few examples, and that may assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have, please -- it's page 20 in English, and I think it's page -- well, it's -- the number at the top is 0094-1353. Page 23. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 30th of April listed violation of cease-fire agreement, Croatian Defence forces. Team from the 5th Corps, Krajina Corps -- 5th Corps Command went to the village. Tactical Group 3, UN vehicle, artillery, so on and so forth. And can with go to the next page, please, in English and the -- two pages on in B/C/S. It records what is described as unusual incidents. Somebody killing somebody. Somebody committed suicide. Somebody injured somebody through careless handling of weapon. All of this in different brigades -- sorry, different units. And then it describes what happened in Banja Luka. There was an explosive device. And, finally, in Prijedor, the SDS Serbian -- the SDS took control -- the SDS forces took control, no armed conflicts so far. Would you agree that's a fairly comprehensive reporting of what went on that day?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, speaking from my practical experience, this is not a combat report. In practice, the heads of duty teams, and I see at the beginning the word "briefing" was mentioned, they are duty-bound to brief the commander each morning, no matter what they had written, about any important events. Or, better put it this way: It looks to me like this officer put done some speaking notes in case the commander should ask him questions based on the report he had received so that he may be in a position to explain. These look like notes for his personal preparation. This is my interpretation of what I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I'm sorry, I didn't intend to suggest it was a combat report. I'm dealing purely with your assertion made in the introduction that there was poor internal communication. And I just want you to look at some examples of this internal communication. Could you have a look now, please, at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or could we have a look, please, at page 26 in English, and it is, I believe -- well, it's 41361; 31 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is part of what was headed on the previous page as: "Briefing at change-over." In fact, I believe it's -- The 343rd Motorised Brigade command dispatched 105-millimetre Howitzers and a field gun anti-armour battery to the Prijedor garrison. "The troops arrived safely and took up ... planned position [sic]." And then we've got some further reporting about that. As I said, if we go back -- or it may be at the top of the page, I'm not sure. Does it say, "briefing at change-over"? No, I think you have to go back one page -- two pages. One page in English, please, and one page in B/C/S. I hope we've got the right thing. Does that say, "briefing at change-over" in B/C/S? Does that say, "briefing at change-over"? Sorry, General, I would just like you to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it says "briefing at change-over." But in practice, I suppose, this was an auxiliary tool of the previous duty officer who hands over duty to the next duty officer, and he wants to inform him of any events on the previous day for the new man to be acquainted with the situation in the units and on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, if I may add, this is communication between two persons. This is this not communication in the VRS, about which I wrote, about information to be passed on from the commander of the Main Staff to the last private in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But, I'm sorry, we've already looked at -- at part of this with the reports up to the Main Staff, reports to the corps. And now we're looking at communication at corps level from its subordinate units, aren't we? Because the entries there reflect the information that the duty team has acquired from subordinate units. That's right, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. I agree with you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the point is, General, this is the corps concerned with the area that you were supposed to be concentrating on for your report, the western area with those municipalities that you listed at the end of your introduction and methodology. And my suggestion to you is that if you had gone through all of these documents you would not have put in that particular paragraph. Because -- well, because I suggest to you that there was good communication from the lower units of this corps to the corps and from the corps through to the Main Staff. And you've not looked, have you, at any of those documents? Now, I agree that's a long and wrapped-up question. So, first of all: You had not seen this document before, had you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, surely you would remember a duty officer's notebook of this length, running to, in translation anyhow, some 86 pages.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have repeatedly said that the documents used for my report can be found in the bibliography.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, then you haven't seen this one before. If you had seen this document and the whole 1st Krajina Corps collection, which, I can assure you, runs to thousands of documents, do you think that you might have changed your mind about the poor internal communications?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I would not have changed my mind, nor would I have changed my position. I tell you that I know what war is and what communication in wartime is like. I'll give you an example --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no. No, I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed out --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is not your witness, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, but this is just a principle. I think the witness should be permitted to give an example what he means. Otherwise it can be taken quite differently, his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is your example related to the facts of this case or what you tell us is your general knowledge of what wartime is like?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is an example of bad or no communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Is it -- I'm sorry. My question is different. Before I let you go on and to give the example, is it related to the facts of this case, not some completely unrelated activity?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wrote, in general terms, about the whole VRS, and I insist that communication was difficult. You are showing an example to counter my assertion only based on the report of the duty team of one corps only. I told you that there were six more operative contingents of that type in the VRS, which you know very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm going to come on to them when we come to your diagram. But are you telling us that you have looked in detail at the records of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, for example?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I took part in a war, and I attended many national and international conferences, and I stand by my position, that, in wartime, both in Afghanistan and in Iraq and in Rome and in Madrid and in Croatia, where commanders from Military Academies from all over the world gathered, I tell you that the problem of communication is a very serious one in any war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely appreciate that, and I'm not -- General, I'm sorry, you misunderstand. I'm not suggesting that communication was easy. What I am suggesting to you, on the evidence of the documents, is that your assertion that the -- there were poor internal communications is not based on any evidence that you yourself have seen. And that, in fact, is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I told you, I would not change the assertions I made in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, General. And -- and -- I accept it would be difficult for you to sit here and say, "I made a terrible mistake." All right. I'm not going to pursue this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I am going to ask that it be admitted as an exhibit. It goes directly to the General's assertion, and it's part of the collection of document, we say, shows that his assertion is misconceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Did you say "no objection" or "objection"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I must object, Your Honours. Because I think the purpose for which Ms. Korner is using this document is reflected in the transcript. I don't see -- she actually -- he confirmed to her the -- the parts of the document which she read on the transcript, and he gave his answers to why he doesn't change his opinion. Therefore, I don't see any particular reason why we should admit another document of, as Ms. Korner says, 89 pages at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, of course, the substance of the document is not what she is relying on. It's merely the fact of what the document reveals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Quite true, Your Honours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm relying on the sub -- I'm entirely relying on the substance to show - and I've only dealt with three pages because it's a long document - to show that there is a wide range of reports coming in not only from the units about military matters, but also about political matters as well. And so to talk about poor internal communication, this is a document which really shows that it's a misconceived application -- assertion by this officer. And he says, But this is different from reporting; I've shown reports from other units. But this document is vital. And -- and Mr. Zecevic may object. This is the witness, not called by him, but called by Mr. Krgovic. And Mr. Krgovic does not object. I mean, I would submit, I know that the Court is loathe to admit documents, but this is a really important document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that Ms. Korner says this document is vital and I'm entirely relying on the substance to show that I have dealt, and so on and so forth. If the document is vital, it should have been on the 65 ter list of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor, and it should have been presented during the -- the -- the Office of the Prosecutor case. Now Ms. Korner is -- is using this opportunity to expand her own case, which, according to the guidance which Your Honours gave during the break, she would need to meet a certain threshold in order to be able to introduce this document as a fresh document, as a fresh evidence. However, I'm sure that this document exists in the files of the Office of the Prosecutor or in the archives quite some time, and this is not something that they just became aware of as a -- as a new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was footnote 190 to Mr. Brown's -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was footnote 190 to Mr. Brown's report. It was never suggested to Mr. Brown at any stage, who is the expert, if nothing else - and I say he's an expert in a great deal - but in the -- what went on in the 1st Krajina Corps. It was never suggested to him that the communications were bad. It's only ever been suggested to the police that the communications broke down. Until this witness arrives. When he asserts, We say, contrary to evidence of which this document is part, that the communications were bad. Or, I'm sorry, poor internal communications. Your Honour, this document fulfils the criteria of any rule of cross-examination and Your Honours' own rules about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours. If the document is a footnote 190 of the Mr. Brown report, which I'm getting the information for the first time at this point because I don't have time to check the Mr. Brown's report, that only amplifies my position. Because the Office of the Prosecutor was given the possibility to introduce all the documents from Mr. Brown's report that they intend to rely on. Now, at this stage, Ms. Korner says, This is a vital document. If -- if Ms. Korner would say that, well, this was an omission of the Office of the Prosecutor, then we might need to discuss that further. But at this point, I don't think -- I don't think it meets the threshold in accordance with the guidances by the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't thought to be important. Your Honours said we didn't have it on our 65 ter list therefore we couldn't produce it, and that's the point. Nobody at that stage had -- the Defence have an obligation to put their case. If their case was, as expressed through this witness, that there was poor internal communications, that document, and many others, would have gone on to our list and been produced. But it wasn't. And it's -- it's a vital document to show that what the General is saying is, as I say, wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we now go back to your report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go back to paragraph 22 on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the report is 31D2. Could I have 31D2, please; page 7. No, wrong page in B/C/S. I want paragraph 22, please, so I imagine that's -- page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that's where you deal with the 1982 Law on All People's Defence. Have you, General, in your researches or in any conferences or chats you've had with other generals, seen one document emanating from the VRS where reference is made to this 1982 Law on All People's Defence, in particular, Article 104?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I cite this article specifically to show that the law provides for the use of police units to carry out combat assignments, and that is why I mention it as a valid law, because it's the highest law of a country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. Well, it was the highest law of the federal state of -- the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But what I'm now asking you is not that. It's whether you have seen in any document that you've looked at coming from the VRS in 1992 which references Article 104 of the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I remember, in the bibliography of my report there is also the RS Law on Defence from June 1992, under which the police is not considered a component of the armed forces. We have already seen numerous examples in the transitional provisions of some other laws, and possibly this one as well, that the laws and regulations of former Yugoslavia shall be applied in the RS too, unless they are in -- unless they run contrary to RS laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I will ask the question one last time. Have you seen in any document, order, report, directive that comes from the VRS during 1992 which says, "in accordance with," or refers to Article 104 of the Law on All People's Defence? And it's a simple -- no. It's a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Allow him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You carry on, General. What -- just answer that question. That's the question I've asked. Not what you want to tell me. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have not found explicit mention of the application of Article 104. But as far as I remember, I saw in General Milovanovic's transcript that he, as the number two man of the army, said that all armies in the area applied their laws and regulations of former Yugoslavia at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- for the moment -- I'm going to come back to General Milovanovic's testimony. But -- I'm asking you about a document, and I think you've given me the answer to that. Right. Now, from what you yourself saw in the documents and any other literature that you have read, is it your assertion to this Trial Chamber that in every single operation that took place in the Krajina the police were resubordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this has to be viewed on a case-to-case basis. From the point of view of military rules and regulations, I offered a model, a template, of what was possible and what was happening in practice; namely, for the police to be part of the contingent of the armed forces. And these cases can be explained based on military rules and regulations rather than based on the Law on Internal Affairs and the rule-book on the powers of MUP officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So is the answer to my question "no," that's not what you're asserting?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as I said, I used this law to try and find a foothold in terms of explaining why police units were used in combat activities and why the commanders had the right to use them in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We know, General, so -- and I don't think you do, that a number of operations, combat operations, were carried out which involved both the use of military and the police. Is it your assertion that in every case where there was a combat operation, even if the police had not been formally resubordinated, they were, in fact, resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wish we could discuss a specific document or a specific incident. We could then use the framework which I provided in my report. We could use the military rules and regulations. Based on that, I could tell you with certainty, because that specific document and that specific incident would clearly show whether a police unit was subordinated to a military commander or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I admit that there is a certain ambiguity in your question. Because I'm unsure of whether you're asking about the existence of or the participation of the police in each and every combat operation that there was; or whether you're asking if, in those cases where the police actually did participate, a formal resubordination had taken place in each and every single case. So there is an ambiguity, because there's a small area which seems not to be covered in one of your questions; namely, were there combat operations in which the police did not take part at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm not asking him that because he doesn't know. I can't, therefore, ask him about specific operations at all because he hasn't got the faintest idea because he's never looked at any. What I'm saying to him is whether his contention is that where there is an operation, for example, let's take the Kozarac one, although maybe not in front of the General, where there was military participation and police, it follows automatically - and let's use the word "participation" - that there must have been a resubordination. And I -- I think he -- he's saying -- it's quite difficult to work out, but I think he's saying it depends on what the documents are, to see whether there is resubordination or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I am going to show you specific documents at a later stage. But do I understand you to say that there have to be documents brought into existence - namely, an order from a commander - asking for, requesting, the use of police and an agreement by the police, at whatever level, that they will be resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, again, we have two questions there. At any rate, there has to be an order issued by the commander whenever a police unit is used for performing combat tasks. That is indisputable. And that is what I've been saying all along. In cases like that, a police unit is subordinated to a military commander, due to the principles of singleness of command and subordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think, and I'm going to put it to you but I want to deal with the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Ms. Korner, the transcript does not reflect the witness's answer, and that is because you are rushing in -- in with your questions before the translation is -- is -- has stopped what he is answering. So I ask that his -- that he repeats his answer and that it's recorded properly, because it's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The translation had stopped, Mr. Zecevic, and I am dependant on the translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then the problem was that -- that if the translation was okay then the -- then the court -- the court recorder didn't finish getting the translation part onto the transcript, and therefore we have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The translation had stopped after "due to the principles of singleness of command and subordination."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let me read what is recorded in -- as answer: That is indisputable and that is what I've been saying all along. In cases like that," and then nothing "a military commander, due to the principles of singleness of command and subordination." Is that what you heard as a translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, obviously the translation is wrong. So therefore I kindly request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again, Ms. Korner. And let's hear the witness's answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I don't know what the question was I asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can give you a hand with that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You probably can, General. All right? Do I -- my question was: "Do I understand you to say that there have to be documents brought into existence - namely, an order from a commander - asking for, requesting, the use of police and an agreement by the police, at what whatever level, that they will be resubordinated?" And you then replied that it was two questions, which I agree. So what was your reply, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Ms. Korner, under the rules there has to exist a document pursuant to which police units are resubordinated. All police units are attached to a military unit in performing combat tasks. Something else I have said a number of times: The manner in which this unit joins a military unit is not that important, but when a police unit joins a military unit it is resubordinated to a military commander, due to the principles of singleness of command and subordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I am going to deal with the whole of resubordination as a totally separate issue. But before we move on to the formation of the VRS, did it occur to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's the final -- before I move on to the next one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you that, owing to the exigencies of what was happening during the conflict, people didn't follow the exact rules that you have described?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what I'm telling and what I'm interpreting is how it should be and what the military regulations say. It's very precise on that. There can be no dual command. There can only be one man who is in command in the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking -- I'm sorry. I'm not talking about dual command. I'm talking about complete adherence to what you have described as the military rules and regulations. Is it conceivable that during a conflict those rules and regulations were not adhered to?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that is quite possible in this war as in any other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've completed that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while the witness is on his way in, the Chamber has a concern. As you would be aware, we are -- this alternating time between trials brings with it its own challenges, and we wonder about the witness that you have scheduled for, not Monday but the one following Monday's witness. We're concerned that that is -- that such witnesses you have scheduled as a witness can be completed by the end of next week. So I don't know how -- how advanced you are on your preparations in that regard, but if you could report on that as soon as you're able to, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've been monitoring these developments myself, bearing in mind the duration of General Kovacevic's evidence, and I'm trying to deal with this in the following way. Next week, I'll try and have one of those 92 bis witnesses over here in order to fill any gaps created in this way. We're working on this, and some of our witnesses still don't have valid passports. So that is one of the problems that we have been coming across. At any rate, I will do my best, and I will be sure to inform the Chamber in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what we were wondering, and obviously Mr. Krgovic and I have been discussing this, is whether there was any prospect that one of the days scheduled for the Haradinaj case would be allocated to this case, the Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, unless you're aware of something that I am not, the scheduling of that case, so far as I'm aware, wouldn't permit that flexibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of that. Only on the basis that two out of the three Judges in the Haradinaj case are here, I would have, rather, thought it was your decision, obviously in consultation Judge Moloto, but I'm merely raising that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we perhaps go into a little bit of detail about the next witness and the one after that. The next witness is the protected witness 003, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And he would take how -- how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't know. The estimate that's been given is six hours for examination-in-chief. I doubled that but, as I pointed out, only because we don't know what he's going, because we have no statement, no proofing note, and, as yet, no list of documents. So we really have no idea what he's going to be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Ms. Korner, it's a little bit odd at first sight that you double. Normally it's the same time as the calling party for a viva voce witness. That's the standard we applied in the Defence -- in your case, in the OTP case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't think, with the greatest respect, that that's quite right. Certainly, for example, as I said, Dr. Nielsen, who was three hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We make -- we make, as for this witness also, we do make an exception for expert witnesses, because that's another matter. But for normal viva voce witnesses, we always apply the standard of the same time for the Defence as the examination-in-chief, same time for cross as for in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully understand that and I accept that. As I say, the reason I'm doubling it is the -- the -- because we really don't know what the witness is going to say. We've identified a large number of documents without knowing what he's going to be saying, and it may well be that the documents we've identified are also being identified by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But even if we take -- even if we take six hours' chief and six hours' cross, so not doubling it but just taking the same time, that makes 12; Mr. Zecevic, or Stanisic Defence, let's add an hour or so; plus procedural matters, then we'll -- very quickly that adds up to four hearings, four days. So if that starts on Monday, we -- we -- there's only Friday left. So the witness after 003, would that be a witness that could reasonably be dealt with in one day, or even in -- or even in two, if we would take the Monday, as you ask? So what -- do we already know who the next witness will be, the witness after 003?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the original list, yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do know that. But that witness is, I'm afraid, likely to take a great deal likely longer than that. So what I'm thinking about is this: If we have a single day left, we complete the previous witness by the previous day, then perhaps I could bring one of the 92 bis witnesses for a brief examination-in-chief, or for a cross instead. And that is what I've been looking into as we speak, to see if I can deal with it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... so that would be -- that would be a witness for, let's say, one day; chief, cross, and re-direct included?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Because the alternative is to have the witness go back home for two weeks and come back. And that's a bad solution; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's simply -- I would say that's highly improbable because the reason that we asked for the 92 bis witnesses to be called, and Your Honours granted, were because there were reasons why their testimony will be tested, what they have to say, with documents. And so I would respectfully suggest that it may be a bit ambitious to say that a 92 bis witness will be finished in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll consider this over the next break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, as we've already established, General, chapter 2 of your report, pages 7 through to 15, are a general dissertation on the JNA, headed, "The Organisation and Tasks of the Armed Forces of the SFRY." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we move, please, to chapter 3, page 16 in the report, 0031D2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In paragraph 46, I've already dealt with what you said in paragraph 45, but in paragraph 46, you say: "The role of the Yugoslav People's Army was to prevent interethnic conflict, armed conflict." On what do you base that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I know that from personal experience. During 1991 and 1992, we were receiving documents from the then-federal military leadership, stating just that. This was the information that I had, and I informed the units about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you reference, please, a document? Could you tell us a document? A date, or from whom.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that's what happened at the time. There were numerous examples. In the various barracks and compounds occupied at the time by the JNA, the JNA protecting the civilian population and everyone. Persons from all of the ethnic groups there were taking shelter in the JNA compounds for fear of being attacked by the many paramilitary units being established at the time. The then-JNA, specifically the air force, used its planes to evacuate and protect a great many civilians from a number of different areas, and assistance was provided to all those for which to leave war-stricken areas and territories, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So the -- is what you're saying the role, as in the practical reality of what it did, as opposed to what its role was as defined in the law?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the JNA at the time under the existing laws was to protect the federal state and its state structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. If we look very briefly -- sorry. If we look very briefly at the Law on National Defence, which is -- I think you've actually got a copy of it, but it's - where is my list? - it's the first document in our binder, which is also L1 in the law library.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, please, to Article -- the second section, Article 99. Page 64 in English and page 4461905 in B/C/S. Article 99, please. Page 17 in B/C/S; 64 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. 99: "The Yugoslav People's Army is a joint armed force of all Yugoslav nations ... nationalities" et cetera. Article 100: "In time of peace, the Yugoslav People's Army, as a segment of the joint armed forces, shall be organised and make preparations as a shock defence force capable of preventing any surprise aggression ... or threat to the country ..." et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the next page in English, please. Next page in English. No. B/C/S, stay where you are. English, please. This is still Article 1 00. Can we go to page 65 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It talks about waging a successful campaign against the enemy, together with the Territorial Defence it shall prepare and have capability to conduct all types of armed struggle, and under all, even the most difficult wartime conditions, the Yugoslav People's Army shall develop and renew its capabilities as a joint armed force for all nations. And then: "In the event of an immediate threat of war and in other emergencies, units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Armies [sic] may, as an exception, be used to carry out tasks in the sphere of social self-protection." And in Article 101 it states that -- what it consists of: the armed -- the land forces, the air force, air defence, and the navy. Now, as we discussed earlier, General, or as you said earlier, effectively the regulations governing the JNA envisaged an outside enemy, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I say straight away that I accept that in documents that the Court has seen the JNA do suggest that their job is to protect -- or prevent interethnic armed conflict. But I'm going to suggest to you, by looking at some of the documents, that the JNA was, in fact, on the side of the Serbs. Do you agree that the JNA Command, in particular, was on the side of or predisposed to assist the Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I am not aware of any document demonstrating that. You have my assertion, and I stand by my assertion, as formulated in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, as I say, I'm going to show you some documents in a moment. Now, going on to paragraph 50 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go back to the report. That's 31D2. And paragraph 50, which is page 17 in English, and I think 16 in B/C/S. Yes, we need to go back - sorry, one page in B/C/S. 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You state that there that: "When the SFRY Presidency adopted a decision on the withdrawal of the JNA," and I dealt with that, "... the Serbian political leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina set out to form its army in the area where the Serbs were in a majority ..." Are you saying that the army only operated in areas where Serbs were a majority?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm talking about the setting up of a new army in the territory of the then-Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, but what you said there is: "The Serbian political leadership set out to form its army in the area where the Serbs were in the majority ..." Is it your contention that the formation of the VRS, the Serbian army, only happened in areas where Muslims were a majority -- sorry, where Serbs were a majority?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, these days, we saw the decision on the setting up of the army and, later on, its establishment structure, which clearly shows the disposition of corps and brigades, and we can clearly tell which area is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, it is a simple question: Are you saying in this paragraph that only in the areas, the municipalities, in which Serbs were a majority did the VRS seek to set up its forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, where in this paragraph can the word "only" be found? If Ms. Korner is quoting, I kindly ask that she quote accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: She's asking for clarification. The way the sentence appears, she's asking the witness to -- as to what -- whether the import is as she interprets it. It's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, General, could I have an answer, please, now. You've had a long time to think about it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I stand by this position. It was possibly unprecise. Because at the time, the borders of Republika Srpska may not have been very clearly defined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did you know -- for example, let's take Bosanski Samac. Did you know that the Serb army was mobilised there, or Serbs were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm not referring to specific events, but, rather, to the fact that after the withdrawal of the JNA a new army was set up in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But were you aware, General, that the Republika Srpska was claiming a number of territories in which they were not in a majority?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, those must have been political decisions. I'm talking about a fact which can easily be verified; namely, that a new army was set up then in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that is not what you said, General. Forgive me. What you said, and I'll read it very carefully for the third time, is: "...the Serbian political leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina set out to form its army in the area where the Serbs were in a [sic] majority ..." Now, if all you meant was that the Serbian leadership set up an army, why did you add those words?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember what made me do that, Ms. Korner. But I know that the tasks of that army and its role were to protect the Serbian people, and these may have been the reasons. Because the other peoples already had their armies set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. That's what you go on to say. And we're going to look at that part, at least as far as the ABiH is concerned. So you can't give any explanation to us why you said "in the areas where the Serbs were a [sic] majority"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you that the task of that army was to protect the Serbian people. And it is logical that it was set up where the Serbs were the majority. Because you couldn't set up a Serbian army without making sure that you can man it from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's complete and utter nonsense, isn't it, General? That it -- that it was set up in -- where the Serbs were in a majority. Do you know what the majority in Prijedor was, for instance?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think that the Muslims were the majority there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite. And we can show you some [indiscernible]. What about in Bosanski Samac? Who was in the majority there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is fair question. The proper question could be where exactly the place where the Republika Srpska army was formed. Which place?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm not prepared to answer Mr. Krgovic's questions, but my suggestion would be that the Serbian army was formed in a number of different places with a number of different corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who was in the majority in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Ms. Korner. I don't know any information about the ethnic make-up of Bosanski Samac, and I don't wish to conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about Brcko?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in Brcko the Muslims were in the majority, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite. Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the relevant information for Donji Vakuf, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Ms. Korner, methinks that the Muslims were in the majority in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: An overwhelming majority, would you agree, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wish to say here that the other two peoples already had their respective armies established and that the Serbian leadership passed the decision to establish their army, the third one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know when the formal establishment of the Army of ABiH took place?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I told you that the date is 15 April. And they celebrate that date, because after the war they often invited me to those celebrations in the Republic of Serbia, which celebration was organised by their embassy and the military attachés.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a look at what actually happened on the 15th of April in a minute. I want to come to the rest of your report, or these paragraphs. And then we'll look at the documents. In paragraph 52, you state that the decision, that is, to set up the Army of the Serbian republic, was adopted based on the constitution of Republika Srpska in response to the situation at the time. And you footnote that as number 14. And your footnote in number 14, effectively, does it not, simply repeats what you said in paragraph 49? Sorry ... actually that's not quite right. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in that footnote, I merely clarify the notion of the current situation, and it may well be that it actually states the same as the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then, can you look, please, at paragraph 56, which is the next page. There, you set out the Law on Defence, which regulates the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Interior. And as you point out, in this law there is no mention of the armed forces or participation of the police units and the RS MUP in the execution of combat tasks in the conditions of imminent threat of war or war. In practice, however, police units of the RS MUP participated in the execution of combat tasks either jointly with the VRS or resubordinated to it. So you do agree, from what you say there, that there are two types of, if you like, action between -- that there are two types of - I'm trying to think of a neutral word for this - co-action, if you like, between the MUP and the VRS; one is either a joint operation, and one is an operation where the police are actually resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when I wrote this, I wanted to point out that during a certain period there was one way of using the police, when the commanders themselves took police forces and resubordinated them, and that is characteristic of the first period in 1992 especially, or, rather, the first half of that year. The other way, which, to my mind, is more correct, was when military commanders sent requests to the chiefs of the security services and asked them for certain forces. But it doesn't really matter, because in both cases the units in question were resubordinated to the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite. The answer you've just given me, I agree. Both ways, whether with or without permission, is resubordination. But that is not what you say there, General. You are clearly making a distinction there between joint activities and resubordinated activities; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I said that, with this, I wanted to point out the varying practice or the different practices during the two periods I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What you've done in your answer there is say, There was a period when military commanders took the police they needed and a period when they asked for permission, as they should have, of the police chief. But that is not what you are saying here, is it, General? You read, please, your own sentence in your own language so that we can make sure that it's correctly translated. Please read out the sentence that begins: "In practice ..."

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, I'm not getting any translation at all. I don't know whether anybody else is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, General. I'm sorry. I'm very sorry, General, please, could you read out the sentence again slowly. Just the sentence, and don't add anything. Please just read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm reading: "However, in practice, police units of the RS MUP participated in the execution of combat tasks, either in co-ordinated action with the VRS units or resubordinated to them."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you're drawing a distinction, aren't you, there between co-ordinated action and resubordination, ergo, General, when you wrote this, you were saying that co-ordinated action is a separate thing from resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I stated here how things went in practice. Co-ordinated action and resubordination are two different activities. But, at any rate, resubordinated units and units in co-ordinated action are subordinated to one commander, which speaks about the command relationship. We already discussed the difference between an action and a relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And I suggest -- General, is it after conversations with Mr. Cvijetic and Mr. Krgovic that you have tried to bring together these two things, co-ordinated action and resubordination, as one thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, I think it is really improper line of question. Because this suggests something like misconduct or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have the same reservation, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the difficulty is that the General has said he had conversations with Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Cvijetic about these reports. My suggestion, regrettable though it is, is that this came about as a result of discussions with the Defence, or I'm asking if that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really think that this is inappropriate. What if I were to say, "Why is Mr. Brown sitting in Ms. Korner's office at -- to assist her to formulate the questions for this witness?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we misunderstand Ms. Korner's question. And if it is -- if what she's suggesting - and we come back to the first day of this witness's cross-examination - that this would have occurred around the time of the preparation of the report, then it is a permissible line. If, however, as I interpreted it, and clearly as counsel for the Defence interpreted it, that it was some improper communication after witnesses were sworn, then it would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry, no. No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- no, no, no, I'm not suggesting that. I am relying on what was said about before the witness was sworn. After the report had been compiled, when he was here, for, I believe, some three or four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now that we know the time-period we're talking about, then you may certainly pursue that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, we are entitled, as the Office of the Prosecutor is, to proof the witness. We did that with the -- with the -- with the witnesses of the Office of the Prosecutor as well. And there shouldn't be any suggestions, if they are not based on -- on some reliable grounds, that the -- that the -- that the counsel for Defence did anything improper in order -- suggesting during the proofing to the witness how he should answer the questions or change his position in the -- establishing the expert report. I don't think that is proper, Your Honours -- that it's proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm making, or I'm asking, because that's all can I do. Because if this is right, there's a total change from what's in the report in this line and what he's now saying. And I'm entitled to ask him whether this change came about as a result of his conferences with Defence counsel before he began testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the difference, Ms. Korner, and you're testifying again. Where is that change? Why don't you simply ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, please continue, Ms. Korner. There is -- and this is something that Ms. -- I recall the first day when this controversy - I would use that term - arose, Ms. Korner, in an aside, said -- talked about the inherent danger of counsel speaking with -- with witnesses beforehand. And there is always a -- and this isn't peculiar to this trial, it isn't peculiar to counsel. It's inherent in the nature of the exercise, that in proofing a witness, the questions that ask for clarification, whatnot, may raise the specter of coaching. But it's something that Ms. Korner, I think, is entitled to explore so that the Chamber knows, at the end of the day, what the quality of the evidence is and to what extent it may have inadvertently or otherwise been influenced by the -- such conversations as they would have had. Please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you accept that in this sentence you are making a distinction - and this is about the fifth time I've asked this question - between co-ordinated action with the VRS, on the one hand, or resubordinated to it, on the other?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner. And I'm saying that it was different in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Because resubordinated means that it is, as the Law on All People's Defence said, under the command of an army. Co-ordinated action, as you distinguish here, does not mean that the police are acting under the command of the army. They are acting jointly or together.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. As I said, in the case of co-ordinated action and in the case of resubordination, there's always one person who is in command and one person who is responsible for the implementation of a specific task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then why do you make the distinction in your report if it doesn't make a ha'p'worth's of difference?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, I'm telling you, in practice there were different ways of reassigning, attaching, and all these other actions. Nevertheless, in my opinion, as I said, this is not important. What I am saying is this: There are rules and there are regulations. No matter what your manner of joining a military unit is, the responsible person is always the commander of that military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but there are combat actions and there are combat actions. In some, I accept, General, the police will be acting as a unit of the military; but in others, they are acting in co-ordination or co-operation by doing the mopping up, providing security. Do you agree there are those distinctions between the types of operations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner. There are distinctions like that. These distinctions are defined in a co-ordinated action plan, whenever we deal with co-ordinated action. Again, any operation is headed by the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you -- you're absolute -- you may be absolutely right on that, but it does not necessarily follow - and unfortunately we're getting on to the subject again, and I'd like to deal with it as one thing - it does not necessarily follow that if there's a military operation which is headed by a military commander, the role of the police within that operation automatically means it is subject to the commands of the military, let's put it, the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is regulated by certain documents, acts, and orders - who, when, where, according to what plan, on what mission, carries out what particular obligation or completes what particular action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree, for the large part, and we're going look at the directives that were issued by the Main Staff for some of the main action. But all, for the moment, I've been concentrating on is that one sentence, and I think, at the end of it, you agree there is a distinction that you are making in this sentence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was -- this question was posed for the nth time, and each and every time the witness answers the same. I think there is at least four answers on precisely the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is obvious that Ms. Korner doesn't understand what witness -- but I don't want to -- to clarify that because it might be understood as coaching the witness. But if the witness is excused, I can explain very easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... no, no, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute, Ms. Korner. Because I, too, have not fully understood the witness's answer. And let me put it to you more directly, General. If there had been a military operation that was, according to the rules, led and commanded by a military officer, if after the completion of the operation, the successful completion of the operation, the military would then cease the hostilities and the police that had joined in a co-ordinated action would then do the subsequent mopping-up, would that still be something that would be done under the command and direction of the military commander, or would it be for the police itself to figure out how to mop up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all of this is done based on a given document; specifically, an order. Such an order determines exactly who does what and according to what plan. For as long as the police unit is within that military unit, the police unit remains under the command of the military commander and performs any tasks ordered by that same military commander. As I have already emphasised, Your Honour, when a police officer goes on a mission like that, he temporarily loses his powers as an authorised official and becomes a fighter, a soldier, until such time as he has returned to his own police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that this goes for resubordination. That is clear. But would it also apply for the police taking part only as a co-ordinated partner and doing subsequent mopping-up of an area that had now been ceased by the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that applies for as long as the mission set has not been completed. There is also a combat operation plan as well as co-ordinated action plan. These plans describe in great detail who does what. These activities unfold as preordained by those plans. And throughout this time the police units remain under the command of the military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, you see, General, the question that I sit back and struggle with is: What happens after the mission has been completed, in the sense that the military operation was designed to seize control over a particular area? Once that had been completed in the sense that there was no more hostile resistance in the area, then the police would, I suppose, be required to -- to ensure that security would be restored in the area and, as we say, to mop up, to -- to do the last cleaning up that would not necessarily -- or that would not involve military forces. And for those activities done by the police, the question that I sit back with is: Under whose control would that be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there is no document saying that the police unit would be dismissed and no longer be part of that military unit, and given that there is a document showing that this police unit joined the military unit in the first place, the police unit always remains subordinated to the commander of that military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Also in cases where the police unit was not resubordinated but only acted as a co-ordinated partner, in what you call co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, this is co-ordinated action. Co-ordination, as such, is a broader concept, where I come from, Your Honour. In such a case, the police unit would be subordinated to the military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid we can't. But, I mean, I'll come back -- come back to this. Can I just stick to the one sentence, because our suggestion is -- well, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the last time, are you making a distinction in that sentence between the two action -- the two methods: co-ordination and resubordination?
