utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this a number of times. Ms. Korner, these are two different ways, and, yes, I do distinguish the two. Two different ways for a police unit to join a military unit, to enter the composition of a military unit. I repeat, however, in both cases, the principles of singleness of command and subordination continue to apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So if it is co-ordination or resubordination, the police unit who is engaged with the military is subject to the command of the military?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Ms. Korner. For as long as the specific task has not been completed, or a specific operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then, first: What is the point of the distinction?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I know very well why you're asking me this. There is a distinction between resubordination and attaching a unit to another unit. That is what I have been trying to explain over the past few days. The commander of a unit has certain powers and certain rights, when something that belongs to him is moved from one component to another --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no, no --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have told us all that at least twice. I understand when the unit in question is an army unit. I'm specifically concentrating on the police. What is the difference, as far as the police are concerned, between -- on what you say there is no difference? So why are there the two terms in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what I'm saying is, the difference consists in the way a unit joins another unit, but there is no difference in terms of the relationship that prevails once a police unit has joined a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have looked at that case where a commander set up the defence of a town. He subordinates all of the forces within that town to his own command. So this is resubordination. We've also looked at a case where a commander seeks from the chief of the public security station that he assigned one of his units to him. It is then that this unit finds itself in co-ordinated action with the military units. In both cases, however, this unit and these men are subordinated to that military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. As we've been through already, General, if there's a request by a military commander to -- for the police to provide men for the purposes of combat, then that is resubordination. We agreed for that. But what you're talking about, and I'm simply concentrating on this one sentence, namely, that either way, whether it's attached, or whatever, what is your basis in law for saying that where a police officer, or police officers, act in co-ordination they are resubordinated and come under the control of the military? Please identify the law that says that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just track down the specific paragraph, Ms. Korner, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm looking at chapter 214 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... do you mean paragraph 214?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph, yes. That is where I find the foothold that I need for my theory. I quote the paragraph, which reads: "The brigade commander has the sole right of exercising command over all units from the composition of the brigade and," I emphasise "any attached units."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... yes, I fully understand that. Except in order for the unit to be attached in the way that you describe the police unit, it has to be resubordinated, because that's what the law says, doesn't it, 104, if it's applied, of the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at all of the rules and regulations, it reads that there can only be a single commander who is in command. And that implies a relationship of subordination. I do believe that it might be somewhat difficult to understand, but that's how it works.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, General, it's not difficult to understand. I suggest that in your capacity and your feeling as a member of the Defence team you have, as you put it, constructed a theory which is not based on either the law or reality that says whenever the police and military act together, the military control what the police does. I suggest there is not one iota of evidence to support what you say.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I was very precise. I never used words such as "whenever." I provided two specific examples from actual practice. If a military commander, on his own, decides to use police units, which actually happened, then he is responsible, and he commands that police units [as interpreted]. The other case: His own direct superior allows him to attach to his own military unit a police unit to be used for a specific assignment. There is only one thing that applies in both cases, and that is what I'm claiming. There is only one commander. In this case, the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. When there are combat operations, as defined what combat means, fighting, when a military commander asks for or is given, although, as you pointed out, the minister of the interior can't just give people to fight, but if police are handed over, under the resubordination principles for combat, then he commands. That is totally different, as, I suggest, you made clear in that report, from co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. In both cases, a police unit is resubordinated to the military commander. Except for cases of co-operation - I emphasise, co-operation. And this is a concept that we've been through, where there is equality between the partners involved. Co-ordinated action is complex and difficult. The most complex form of co-operation in combat that there is. I have provided a number of examples of possible errors --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... let's not get sidetracked.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the fact that there is only a single person in command is meant to prevent precisely those errors from occurring.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we -- it's -- we're past the usual time for the break. Could we return to this in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I would ask you to keep an eye on the clock because we have to rise at 6.55 today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to come back, as I say, later to resubordination, but I want to move through a couple more paragraphs of your report. Could you have a look, please, now at the diagram that you did. Page 20. It comes directly after paragraph 61 in English. It's -- it's, in fact, 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 61, please. 61. And could we have the same diagram, please, in B/C/S possibly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a, sort of, generic diagram of the make-up of the VRS; is that right, General? Organisation.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Am I right also in thinking that although your report says it was concentrating on the western area of indictment, which was the area covered by the 1st KK, you made no attempt to -- to break down the components of the 1st KK itself?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this paragraph of my report deals with the organisation of the VRS as a whole. That is why I used this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. But did you at any stage consider that it might be helpful to have a more in-depth look at the 1st KK and a diagramatic representation of how it was?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that could have been included, too. But here I decided to talk about the overall organisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In fact, you took that diagram from your report from the Popovic case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner. I think that is the same diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I just want to ask you about a couple of things that are omitted from this that were included in your original Popovic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So could we have up -- sorry, the Popovic report at page 11 in English. And the Popovic report is 20232, please. Tab 100. Could we have the B/C/S of the Popovic report, please, too. I think the pages are much the same. Yep. Thank you. No, that's -- is that the same? No, that's a different one, please. Can we see what the page number is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just -- General, hold on. Oh, I see you -- yes. Okay. Thank you, General. What's the page number?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we've got it. Thank you very much. All right. First of all, you give a key, which you omitted from the present report, to the names of the corps. I don't think that's important. But I want to know why you omitted the figures in your present report. Under 1 KK, we see Division 1; 79 brigades; 19 regiments. Why was it that you omitted those figures from your present diagram?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I dealt here with the organisational levels, and I wanted to show the strategic level of organising and also the operative and tactical level. I cannot remember why I left the figures out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, was it because if you'd put the figures in it showed that the VRS, in terms of its structure and make-up, was considerably greater in size than the ABiH or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. As for the subject that I studied in my reports, I claim that the relative size of the army is not what really counts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I also put to you that the VRS had far greater fire-power, in terms of weaponry and aircraft, than either the ABiH or the HVO in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have a reference for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I put it to you, General? Would you accept that that is so?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we would have to make a specific comparison that would require serious analysis. You may be right, but I didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't going to, but I suppose I ought to take you to the part of a report you have read, which is the combat readiness report in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please - yes, thank you - it is document ... 8-- P1781. And can we go, in 1781, to -- I think it's page 69 in English. Yes. We can start at page 69. Page 62 in the B/C/S. 69 in English; 62 ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the paragraph that's near the end of the page: "Thanks to the vigorous opposition of the commander and the entire Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, to the decision of the competent authorities of the FRY army to withdraw combat hardware, the pullout of most of the combat hardware together with the personnel - the FRY nationals - was prevented." Do you agree that in effect the JNA handed over its combat hardware and personnel to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, based on the paragraph you've read out, that would be the conclusion to draw. But I insist that the quantity of weapons is not what matters, but, rather, whether by using those weapons you violated the provisions of the international laws of war. Ms. Korner, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was attacked by some 25 countries, as is generally known, during the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no, no, no. I am going to stop you there because we're getting really sidetracked. And, General, I'm not suggesting at this stage - that's a matter for the Court - whether the weapons were used in violation of international laws of war. Can I make that clear. All, at the moment, I'm trying to get you to -- to deal with, with you, is that the VRS was considerably superior to the other armies in the conflict, in terms of weaponries, supply, and manpower. Now, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I agree with you, although it is extremely important to make a comprehensive analysis that takes into consideration all relevant information in order to claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I would also suggest to you, and I don't want to take you through it, that the same statements, effectively, appear in the corps -- in the one -- the 1st Krajina Corps report of the combat readiness, which was prepared. I'm not going to take you through that, as I say. Now, all right. So, dealing with the diagram, you say you didn't leave it out deliberately. You just level it out because? That's a question. Why did you leave it out?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to turn, now, to looking at the documents about the formation, or how it came about, of the VRS, which you have said came about entirely -- well, are you saying that? Can I just confirm that: Are you saying that the VRS was formed only because the Muslims had formed the ABiH and the Croatians had formed the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS was established pursuant to the decisions of the then-state authorities, Ms. Korner. I state as much in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But you -- you say, in fact, you say it twice in your report, and we've looked at the paragraphs, that the VRS was formed because - and that was paragraph 50, which we dealt with before the break - because the Muslim and Croatian armies had already been forged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please read the whole paragraph, including the sentence the Prosecutor has left out. Maybe it can be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have actually been through this paragraph. "When the SFRY Presidency adopted a decision on the withdrawal of the JNA, the Serbian political leadership in BiH set out to form its army in the area where the Serbs were in a majority ..." I spent some time on that. "... because Muslim and Croatian armies had already been formed." And I believe you say it elsewhere. Yes, you do. You say it in your footnote. You repeat paragraph 50 in your footnote 14. Now, is it your contention that the VRS was formed by the -- the Serbian leadership only because the Muslim and Croatian armies had been formed, according to you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I used this information to highlight that the VRS was established only after the other two armies had already been set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. But -- that's still not quite the answer to my question. I'm sorry. Are you saying it was merely something you noted in passing, or that the reason for the setting up of the VRS is those two armies?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the key reason for the establishment of the VRS was the fact that the only regular army at the time, the JNA, was withdrawing from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Serbian people who wanted to remain in the framework of a Federation did not have an armed force. Therefore, to protect that people, the state authorities took that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was an entirely defensive, as opposed to offensive, decision; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I said that the decision was taken as was fit, given the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that's a very interesting answer, but it's not an answer, again, to my question. Is it your contention, having studied this part of the conflict, that the VRS was set up as a defensive or an offensive? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, terms such as "defensive" or "offensive" are used to point out an aspect of combat activity, whether it's an attack or defence. Here, I'm saying that the VRS was established to protect and defend the Serbian people at a time when it felt threatened, and it had been left -- or it was left without a regular army that was withdrawing from the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you entertain a suggestion that it was the Muslims and Croats who were terrified of what was going to happen in early 1992 because of what had already happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I stated a fact. The fact that the other two peoples had established their own armies. You should ask them why their authorities at the time decided that they didn't want to stay in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I don't think that's the point at all. What I'm talking about is violence; but, anyhow, let's look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, document 20226, which is document 3 in our list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the copy - or a copy - of the directive of the Federal Secretary for National Defence on the use of armed forces, dated the 10th of December, 1991. Have you ever seen that before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this document is something I don't think I have seen. But I'll try to correct you; this document speaks about the use of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... I'm so sorry --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... I don't follow what correction you're making.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm trying to say that, as far as I can tell, this document was only sent to one command rather than to the entire armed forces. It was sent to only one corps. And, at the time, the JNA could have up to 30 corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thank you. However, this is, as you say, the 9th Corps of the JNA. And this is a directive from the federal secretary. This is the -- the -- the JNA, you say, was there to prevent interethnic conflict and protect all peoples. And we went through that when we looked at the JNA. Could you look, please, at the second page of this directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would be the third page, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war: Protection of the Serbian population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis ..." and so on and so forth. The federal secretary there is saying to this corps of the JNA, which is supposed to be all people's corps, it is there to protect the Serbian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I feel I must explain this fact. This document, as far as I remember, was sent to the Knin Corps. And the territory that made up its zone of responsibility was mostly populated by Serbs. I remember the political message that was sent to two sides. The one side was the then-Croatian military leadership. And the message for them was, If you attack these people, the Yugoslav People's Army will protect them. On the other hand, this was also a message for the Serbian people, that they should not set up their open paramilitary units because the JNA will protect the Serbs against any possible threat. What is also very important, Ms. Korner - and during that period, I was in the Republic of Croatia - the Serbian people in the Republic of Croatia, under the federal constitution that was in force then and the constitution of Croatia, was a constituent people, which means that without the political will of that people, the political system in that country could not be changed, if I understand the notion of constituent people correctly. This is how I interpret this document, which was used for propaganda purposes to show that the JNA was only protecting the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are you saying you have seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. But it seems to me that it was published at the time, because the then-federal leadership still included members of various peoples, as far as I remember. And as soon as a document is adopted, it immediately leaks and is used for various purposes in accordance with one's preferences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you not think - and that's all I want to ask you about - that it would have been more appropriate if the order had said, "The protection of all peoples under threat"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking my mind, and I'm saying why I think that this was phrased this way. It is a known fact that 200.000 Serbs were expelled from that area. Obviously the Yugoslav People's Army did not protect that population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Can we move, now, to -- forward in time to the 20th of March, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at document 01976. Tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document from General Kukanjac, who was the general in charge, was he not, of the 2nd Military District, until he was removed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner. In the signature block of this document, we read, "General Kukanjac."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is -- it doesn't actually say what it is. It's an evaluation, in the second -- in the first paragraph: "We are kindly asking you to return these documents after use. For justified reasons, we are suggesting to present this document to the smallest circle of people as necessary."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now go, please, to paragraph 5. Volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd Military District, which is page 6 in English. And it's page 6 in B/C/S as well, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there's obviously a map. And then it talks about, in paragraph (d), number of people in the zones of the - "corpses" I think not - I think it is "corps." And then, at paragraph (f): "The JNA distributed 51.900 pieces of armament, (75 per cent), and the SDS, 17.298 pieces." Would you accept that the JNA or that General Kukanjac is saying that they distributed weaponry to the Serbs in March?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. This is what it says. Although I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And in Sarajevo, 300 automatic rifles have been distributed so far, to the retired officers. And for three or four days there'll be a hundred armed people they will defend, protect. Residential areas. Would you agree from the context that these 300 automatic rifles in Sarajevo have been distributed to retired Serb officers?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Should I go back -- and we're going to look at another document in a minute -- wasn't it right that the JNA was on the side of the Serbs? It was already, effectively, its army.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I told you that, just like in Croatia, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Serbian people was equal to the two other peoples, and it was one of the constituent peoples. Without their political will, the other two peoples decided to leave the Federation, to break away. And the Serbian people, as far as I remember, had, as its political option, staying in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to enter into the argument now about the referendum against the plebescite and all the rest of it. But what I'm concerned about, what I'm asking you about, is, the JNA was supposed to be an army of all the peoples but what it was doing was arming the Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Specify when it says "army." Particular corps or army, JNA, general.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you want to answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I've already said this. The other two peoples did not accept the JNA, which was still the regular military force there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It -- whether it accepted the JNA or not, the JNA was quite deliberately arming non-military people, effectively, as -- to be used against the other constituent peoples in Bosnia; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a single example of what happened in the area of responsibility of that corps. What I know from practical experience in Croatia is that the families of military personnel and the whole residential buildings in which they lived were surrounded and besieged by the paramilitary units of the Croatian army at the time. I suppose that these were distributed in a bid to protect precisely those families.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why? Why do you suppose that, as opposed to it being an offensive distribution to be used to take over territory that was not populated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I believe that the weapons were distributed primarily to protect the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... yes. I --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This effort was based on historical precedents from earlier wars.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's not waste any more time. Can we look at one further paragraph, please, which is at the top of page 8 in B/C/S, under paragraph 6: Warehouses of war equipment ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, page 6 in English, please. Next page in English and next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph that begins: "Reserves of material (9.930 barrels and 200 tonnes of ammunition) from the Territorial Defence, from the joint warehouse Rabic, near Derventa, to be transferred to Banja Luka," although on the map Ugrinski Lug is already shown "because the part of the material will be temporarily stocked there. The (secret) action of the transfer is in course." So, secretly, large quantities of ammunition were being transferred by the JNA to Banja Luka. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree, Ms. Korner. I don't know the reason behind it, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, on what happened later, General, the reason was to take over territories by force that did not contain Serb majorities.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I told you, based on my practical experience in Slovenia and Croatia, the armies being organised at the time were attacking JNA storage facilities and warehouses, taking away weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this document also be exhibited. It was produced in order to deal with his contention that the JNA -- or -- there is no support of the Serbs from the JNA, as opposed to any other army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's completely irrelevant for this case. It was said because -- I turn on Serbian. [Interpretation] Where in his report does the witness say anything about weapons, about warehouses, about how weapons were distributed? I think this bears no relevance to our present case at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's dealt with because the whole tenure of the General's report about the formation of the VRS is that this was no more than a response to the formation -- the formation of the Army of ABiH and the HVO, and this document shows that, effectively, way before that, the Serb army was being helped created, if you like, by the provision of supplies and weaponry from the JNA. And, equally, his assertion that the JNA was not on the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, Your Honours, if that is the Prosecutor's position in their case, they should have stated so in their pre-trial brief so we can provide the -- the adequate response during our Defence case, that we are on notice that this is the Prosecutor's case. Because, so far, we never understood that this is a part of the Prosecutor's case, who was and at what time were the armies formed and who was supplying which ammunition and the -- and -- and the weapons to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have -- I'm so sorry, but that is utterly misleading. We have always said that the JNA was responsible for arming the Serbs. It is in our pre-trial brief. We've raised this question of which army was formed first during -- or it was raised by the Defence, and we have always made it clear that we did not accept that the armies of ABiH and HVO, as such, were created at an early stage, such as this. So it's quite, quite misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. But the question still arises as to why wasn't this document tendered during the presentation of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, because, Your Honour, we didn't have a General saying -- we didn't have a report saying that the VRS is only formed as a result of the formation of the -- the other armies. And, Your Honours, this document has been disclosed forever and ever and ever. So it's not a question as though it wasn't -- that the Defence weren't -- knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we have a look, please, at a document of the following day, the 1st of April, which is document 20-- oh, sorry, not the next day. Ten days later. 20227, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 17th Corps, 1st of April, to the 2nd Military District Command. "During the 31st of March," and this is paragraph 4, "to the 1st of April, the conflict escalated in the area of Bijeljina. According to unverified information, Arkan's people entered Bijeljina. In the part of the town where the Muslims reside, the barricades were erected. The passage to the town is blocked. In the town, explosions and rifle fire can be heard." Now, do you know about the fact --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... oh, I'm sorry. There you go, I'm sorry. I didn't realize it. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... have a read of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, paragraph 88, for you, of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. General, have you read that part?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You know about, don't you, Arkan's Men going into Bijeljina and killing and terrorising the Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that this paramilitary unit was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you think, from what you're saying, it was the duty of the JNA to prevent Arkan's Men from attacking the town in this way and killing the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But they didn't, did they? They just stood by and watched and did nothing. They reported it to the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is, indeed, what happened, and I can't judge, myself, based on this dispatch, then the commander of that unit, in that area, should have prevented the paramilitary units committing those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you would expect, wouldn't you, if he'd done anything about it, for him to report in this report, We are taking the following action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to this line of questioning. Is Ms. Korner testifying here about the murders committed by Arkan? What exactly are these questions based on? And why about this particular situation? Where exactly does the document say they killed or massacred such and such a number of people, or is Ms. Korner, indeed, testify to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm pretty certain we've got evidence in about this somewhere. But I'll change the nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If, during the course of the attack on Bijeljina by Arkan, which is reported here - and I think we -- yes, we will find -- in fact, the evidence is coming in a minute - you would have -- and if this commander had done anything to stop it, you would have expected him to report it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it in no uncertain terms. Where does the document indicate that an attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going -- I'm not even going to deign to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the commander was going to do any -- had done anything, General, you would have expected it to have been in this report, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we look, please, then, at the next report, the following day, which is document 6A, 2024--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, yes, General. The General is indicating something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I think he'd like some water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have up - I think I did say - document 20227. Tab 6 -- no, tab ... sorry. Yes, tab 6. No, tab 6A. 20 -- sorry, 20246.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the following day. And in paragraph 2 he talks about this waiting generates tension with conscripts. In order to strengthen the forces in the Bijeljina garrison, 3 tanks, et cetera. One truck carrying soldiers. And after the conflict ... Right. Then after paragraph 4, oh, well, paragraph 4: [As read] "The situation in the area is still very complex ... was the worst situation in Bijeljina at present. After heavy fighting, and at around 9.30 the situation calmed down ... on the 2nd of the 4th, the party leaders do not control the situation and are not capable of stopping the activity. For this reason they are not able to even enforce the curfew set for between 8.00 and 6.00, and the MUP at present refuse to participate in mixed patrols with JNA. So far we know of three persons killed, 15 to 20 wounded ... but it is certain there are more killed and wounded than that. And the road leading from Bijeljina to Zvornik is blocked in places ..." Would you agree this is still talking about the incursion of Arkan and his men into Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we don't see that specifically here, as we did in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But it's clear, isn't it, that he's talking about Bijeljina. He's talking about the people waiting in the -- the garrison, the re -- I mean, the increasing in the strength of the armaments.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, based on this, it is impossible to say who of the warring parties are in this conflict, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... let's look, we'll see for sure in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 8, please; page 2 in English, and I think it's page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The situation in the zone of the corps is very unfavorable. The situation is especially difficult in Bijeljina, where the armed conflict between the citizens of Serb and Muslim ethnicity continues. The corps command engaged part of 336 motor brigade forces in order to strengthen the defence of the barracks, although the barracks have not been attacked so far ... no fighting in ... Brod and Derventa ..." Now, again, by the next day, the JNA unit there has done nothing to prevent the interethnic conflict, has it? What it's done is reinforce its own barracks.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the reasons, Ms. Korner. Was that unit or command also under siege in one way or the other? What were its tasks at the time? I don't know. It is difficult for me to judge this particular action. Nevertheless, I do agree, if, indeed, the unit was in a position to stop any interethnic clashes from breaking out, it should have done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take -- we take the adjournment, to reconvene tomorrow afternoon. There are two things in terms of scheduling that we would point out before we rise. One is that Mr. -- in terms of the witness scheduled to begin on Monday, the -- our own projection is such that, Mr. Krgovic, there would be -- it appears to us that the -- that witness's testimony will, in all likelihood, extend into Thursday. And let me say, parenthetically, that notwithstanding the Prosecution's indication that they need double the amount of time allocated for the examination-in-chief, that in consistent with our usual practice of being given -- as -- as a basis, the equivalent amount of time, that testimony is likely to extend into Thursday, and we should reserve Friday as a possible spillover day. And therefore it would not be prudent, having regard to the fact that this trial would then be in a two-week recess, to take another witness for next week. And in terms of the witness at present on the stand, we would require, Ms. Korner, that you complete your cross-examination by the end of the first session on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of September, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m.,
